questions.stem: A 31 year old man has 6 days of nausea, anorexia and dark urine, then yellow eyes. He ate oysters at a beach restaurant in Thailand 4 weeks ago. He has had no new sexual partners. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. His liver is palpable and slightly tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Shellfish in a developing country 4 weeks earlier (incubation 2 to 6 weeks), hepatomegaly without fever and an ALT-dominant picture point to hepatitis A.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Faeco-oral exposure, short incubation, afebrile hepatitis with hepatomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute hepatitis A.

elim: Incubation over 2 months, spread by blood or sex.
Blood-borne and usually asymptomatic when acute.
Mild unconjugated jaundice with a normal ALT.
High fever, myalgia and renal failure after fresh water exposure.

steps.x: **A. Acute hepatitis A.** Shellfish/travel + 2–6 week incubation + afebrile hepatitis = hepatitis A.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man from Hampshire has 1 week of flu-like aches, loose stools and then jaundice. He has not travelled. He makes his own sausages and often eats pork that is pink in the middle. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg. His liver is tender and enlarged. Hepatitis A IgM and hepatitis B surface antigen are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Undercooked pork can transmit hepatitis E, which gives a flu-like illness with jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and sometimes diarrhoea.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: pork that is pink in the middle
flu-like aches, loose stools and then jaundice
steps.x: Raw or undercooked pork, flu-like prodrome, diarrhoea and jaundice, with HAV and HBV negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute hepatitis E.

elim: Blood-borne; rarely causes a symptomatic acute illness.
Diarrhoea, but not jaundice with tender hepatomegaly.
Needs existing hepatitis B; HBsAg is negative.
Chronic cholestatic disease with itch, not acute illness.

steps.x: **B. Acute hepatitis E.** Undercooked pork + flu-like illness + jaundice = hepatitis E.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man who has sex with men has 2 weeks of joint pains and an itchy, raised rash, then jaundice. He had condomless anal sex with several partners 3 months ago. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. His ALT is 1800 IU/L (10–50). Serology is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
questions.e: HBsAg with anti-HBc IgM means acute hepatitis B; HBeAg and high HBV DNA show high infectivity.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: joint pains and an itchy, raised rash
steps.x: High-risk sexual exposure, incubation over 2 months, urticaria and arthralgia prodrome, IgM core antibody.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute hepatitis B.

elim: Needs HBsAg for over 6 months with anti-HBc IgG.
Needs HDV antibodies and pre-existing hepatitis B.
HBsAg would be negative.
Gives anti-HBs only, with no HBsAg or anti-HBc.

steps.x: **A. Acute hepatitis B.** HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM = acute hepatitis B; HBeAg + DNA = highly infectious.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman from Ghana has blood tests before starting rituximab. She feels well and has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B. Her ALT is 28 IU/L (10–50). Her hepatitis B results are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
o: Past hepatitis B infection, now cleared
questions.e: Negative HBsAg with anti-HBc IgG and anti-HBs means past infection that has cleared; vaccination gives anti-HBs alone.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Core IgG present, surface antigen absent, surface antibody present, normal ALT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Past hepatitis B infection, now cleared.

elim: Needs HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM.
Needs HBsAg positive for over 6 months.
Core and surface antibodies together fit a real past infection.
Vaccine contains surface antigen only, so anti-HBc would be negative.

steps.x: **D. Past hepatitis B infection, now cleared.** Anti-HBc IgG + anti-HBs, HBsAg negative = past cleared infection.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has had chronic hepatitis B since childhood and has not attended follow-up for 8 years. He has lost 7 kg in 3 months and has a dull right upper quadrant ache. He has a hard, irregular liver edge. His alpha-fetoprotein is 2400 kU/L (<10). Ultrasound shows a 6 cm liver mass.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic hepatitis B progresses to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; a very high AFP with a liver mass is HCC.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Long-standing hepatitis B, weight loss, a hard liver and a mass with a very high AFP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatocellular carcinoma.

elim: Gives fever and rigors.
Benign, incidental, with a normal AFP.
Possible, but AFP is not raised this much and hepatitis B is the risk.
Fluid-filled and benign, normal AFP.

steps.x: **C. Hepatocellular carcinoma.** Chronic HBV + liver mass + high AFP = hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has 1 year of tiredness. She received a blood transfusion in Pakistan after childbirth 30 years ago. She drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. Her BMI is 24. Her ALT has been 110 to 140 IU/L (10–50) on three tests over a year. Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hepatitis C is spread mostly by blood; a transfusion in an endemic area decades ago with fatigue and a persistently raised ALT points to chronic hepatitis C.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Blood exposure years ago, vague fatigue, a chronically raised ALT, HBsAg negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic hepatitis C.

elim: 4 units a week is too little.
Excluded by a negative HBsAg.
Acute only; never chronic.
Unlikely with a BMI of 24.

steps.x: **C. Chronic hepatitis C.** Old blood exposure + vague fatigue + persistently raised ALT = chronic hepatitis C.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man who injects heroin has 1 week of jaundice, vomiting and drowsiness. He had no known liver disease. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg. His ALT is 3600 IU/L (10–50) and INR 1.9. HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM are positive. Anti-HDV IgM is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Hepatitis D superinfection on chronic hepatitis B
questions.e: Simultaneous acute HBV (anti-HBc IgM) and HDV infection is co-infection; HDV makes the illness more severe and faster.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
IVDU, acute HBV markers and HDV antibodies together, with a severe illness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitis B and D co-infection.

elim: IgM anti-HAV would be positive, and no faeco-oral exposure.
HDV antibodies show a second virus.
Would need anti-HCV and is usually silent.
Superinfection needs known chronic HBV with anti-HBc IgG, not IgM.

steps.x: **D. Hepatitis B and D co-infection.** Acute HBV (anti-HBc IgM) + anti-HDV = co-infection; known chronic HBV + new HDV = superinfection.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman at 33 weeks of pregnancy has acute hepatitis E, confirmed 4 days ago after travel to Bangladesh. She is now confused and has bruising. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Her INR has risen from 1.2 to 2.8 and glucose is 3.0 mmol/L.

visual.title: Over 4 days
visual.caption: INR climbing above 1.5 with confusion: acute liver failure.

questions.q: Which complication has most likely developed?
questions.e: Hepatitis E is particularly severe in the third trimester, with a much higher risk of fulminant acute liver failure: encephalopathy and an INR over 1.5.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Third-trimester hepatitis E, now encephalopathic and coagulopathic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute liver failure.

elim: The cause is already known: hepatitis E.
Needs hypertension and proteinuria with haemolysis.
Itch without encephalopathy or coagulopathy.
Would not explain the INR of 2.8.

steps.x: **B. Acute liver failure.** Hepatitis E in the third trimester → high risk of fulminant liver failure.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman at 14 weeks of pregnancy is found to have chronic hepatitis B on booking bloods. She is well. Her BP is 110/68 mmHg and pulse rate 80 bpm. Her HBeAg is positive and HBV DNA is high. She asks how likely it is that her baby will be infected without any intervention.
questions.q: Which is the most likely risk of vertical transmission?
questions.e: HBeAg-positive mothers have about a 90% risk of transmitting hepatitis B to their baby without intervention; HBeAg and high DNA mean high infectivity.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
HBeAg positive with a high viral load = highly infectious.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: About 90%.

elim: Far too low for an HBeAg-positive mother.
Closer to the risk in HBeAg-negative mothers.
Underestimates the risk.
Underestimates the risk.

steps.x: **E. About 90%.** HBeAg-positive mother = about 90% vertical transmission risk.

questions.stem: A 33 year old nurse has HIV, diagnosed 2 years ago. She completed a full course of hepatitis B vaccination for her job. Her anti-HBs level 2 months after the last dose is 4 mIU/mL (protective level 10 or more). Her colleagues all responded. She has never had hepatitis B.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for her poor response?
o: Hepatitis B vaccine contains live virus
HIV co-infection blunting the vaccine response
She has occult chronic hepatitis C
The vaccine needs a booster at 10 years
Vaccine given into fat rather than muscle
questions.e: HIV co-infection may blunt the antibody response to hepatitis B vaccination.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: full course of hepatitis B vaccination
steps.x: Immune suppression from HIV, a full course, and a sub-protective antibody level.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HIV co-infection blunting the vaccine response.

elim: The vaccine is recombinant surface antigen, not live.
Not a recognised cause.
Irrelevant 2 months after the course.
Can reduce response, but her known HIV is the stronger reason.

steps.x: **B. HIV co-infection blunting the vaccine response.** HIV can blunt the hepatitis B vaccine response.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with chronic hepatitis B has 2 months of weight loss, testicular pain and a lacy purple rash on his legs. His BP is 172/100 mmHg and pulse rate 84 bpm. He has a left wrist drop. His creatinine is 168 μmol/L (60–110). ANCA is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication of his hepatitis B?
questions.e: Hepatitis B is associated with polyarteritis nodosa: hypertension, renal impairment, mononeuritis multiplex and livedo reticularis, with negative ANCA.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
HBV, livedo reticularis, hypertension, mononeuritis multiplex, renal impairment, ANCA negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Polyarteritis nodosa.

elim: c-ANCA positive with sinus and lung disease.
Would not explain mononeuritis and livedo.
Purpuric rash in children with IgA deposits.
Usually young women, ANA positive.

steps.x: **D. Polyarteritis nodosa.** Chronic HBV + mononeuritis multiplex + livedo + hypertension = polyarteritis nodosa.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man was found to be anti-HCV and HCV RNA positive 20 years ago but never attended for treatment. He drinks 4 units of alcohol a week. He now has abdominal swelling, spider naevi and a palpable spleen. His albumin is 29 g/L (35–50), platelets 70 × 10⁹/L (150–400) and INR 1.5. Ultrasound shows a small, nodular liver with ascites.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cirrhosis from untreated chronic hepatitis C
questions.e: Hepatitis C is curable, but untreated chronic infection causes inflammation-driven fibrosis and cirrhosis, here decompensated with ascites.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: spider naevi and a palpable spleen
steps.x: Untreated chronic HCV for 20 years with stigmata of chronic liver disease and a cirrhotic liver.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cirrhosis from untreated chronic hepatitis C.

elim: 4 units a week is too little.
Would give a large, congested liver, not a small nodular one.
Usually a woman with itch and a cholestatic picture.
Raised JVP and a large liver, not spider naevi or a small nodular liver.

steps.x: **C. Cirrhosis from untreated chronic hepatitis C.** Untreated chronic hepatitis C → fibrosis → cirrhosis (and HCC); DAAs cure it.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy has 5 days of jaundice and poor appetite. Two children in his school class had the same illness last month. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. His liver edge is palpable. His ALT is 1400 IU/L (10–50).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
questions.e: Acute hepatitis A is diagnosed with anti-HAV IgM; IgG shows past infection or vaccination.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: Two children in his school class
steps.x: Outbreak in a school (faeco-oral spread) with acute hepatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-HAV IgM.

elim: Shows past infection or immunity, not acute disease.
Hepatitis C is blood-borne and rarely acute and symptomatic.
IgG shows past exposure; IgM is used for acute hepatitis E.
Tests for hepatitis B, which does not spread like this.

steps.x: **B. Anti-HAV IgM.** Acute hepatitis A = anti-HAV IgM.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has 4 days of jaundice and fatigue after drinking well water while trekking in Nepal. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Anti-HAV IgM is negative. Her ALT is 1200 IU/L (10–50).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic test?
questions.e: Hepatitis E, from contaminated water, is diagnosed with anti-HEV IgM; it matters most in pregnancy.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Contaminated water in an endemic area, hepatitis A excluded, pregnant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-HEV IgM.

elim: Shows immunity to hepatitis B, not current infection.
Hepatitis C is blood-borne.
Only tested if HBV positive.
Invasive and unnecessary when serology is diagnostic.

steps.x: **D. Anti-HEV IgM.** Suspected hepatitis E = anti-HEV IgM.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has had stable chronic hepatitis B for 6 years. He has recently started injecting drugs. Over 2 weeks his ALT has risen from 45 to 920 IU/L (10–50) and he is jaundiced. His HBV DNA is low. Hepatitis A, C and E tests are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Hepatitis D antibodies are tested only in HBV-positive patients; a flare with low HBV DNA after injecting suggests HDV superinfection.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Known HBV with a new flare and low HBV DNA after a new blood-borne risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitis D antibodies.

elim: He is HBsAg positive, so this adds nothing.
Autoimmune hepatitis is unlikely with a clear exposure.
Does not explain an acute flare.
Not the first step; serology will show the cause.

steps.x: **D. Hepatitis D antibodies.** Flare in chronic HBV with new risk = test HDV antibodies.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has 1 week of malaise and jaundice. He has a new partner and has recently travelled to Spain. He drinks 10 units of alcohol a week. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. His ALT is 1650 IU/L (10–50), AST 1200 IU/L (10–40) and ALP 140 IU/L (25–115). Ultrasound is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
o: Viral hepatitis screen of serology and PCR
questions.e: An ALT-dominant hepatitis with several possible exposures needs a viral hepatitis screen combining serology with PCR, the gold standard.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Hepatocellular picture, sexual and travel risk, normal ultrasound.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral hepatitis screen of serology and PCR.

elim: Tests for PBC, which is cholestatic.
Adds nothing after a normal ultrasound.
Invasive and not first-line.
Images bile ducts; the picture is not cholestatic.

steps.x: **E. Viral hepatitis screen of serology and PCR.** Hepatocellular LFTs + exposure = viral hepatitis screen (serology + PCR).

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has finished a 12 week course of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir for chronic hepatitis C. She feels well. Her BP is 124/80 mmHg and pulse rate 72 bpm. Her ALT is now 30 IU/L (10–50). She asks how the team will know she is cured.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test?
o: HCV RNA 12 weeks after the end of treatment
questions.e: Cure is a sustained virological response: undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after finishing therapy.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: 12 week course of sofosbuvir and velpatasvir
steps.x: Treated hepatitis C; cure is judged by viral load after treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HCV RNA 12 weeks after the end of treatment.

elim: Antibody stays positive for life after infection.
Only used to choose treatment.
Invasive and does not measure the virus.
Normal LFTs do not prove viral clearance.

steps.x: **C. HCV RNA 12 weeks after the end of treatment.** Hepatitis C cure = SVR: undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after DAAs.

questions.stem: A 35 year old sex worker attends a sexual health clinic for screening. She feels well and has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test for current hepatitis B infection?
questions.e: HBsAg shows current infection (acute or chronic); anti-HBc IgM shows acute infection and HBeAg shows high infectivity.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
High-risk, asymptomatic, needs a test for any current infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: HBsAg.

elim: Positive only in acute infection; misses chronic carriers.
Shows immunity, not infection.
Shows infectivity in those already HBsAg positive.
Not a screening test.

steps.x: **D. HBsAg.** Current hepatitis B infection = HBsAg.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has acute hepatitis A confirmed by anti-HAV IgM after a trip to Morocco. He is jaundiced and tired but eating and drinking. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. His INR is 1.1 and he is fully alert. He asks about treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Supportive care at home with review of LFTs
questions.e: Acute hepatitis A is self-limiting and resolves in 2 to 3 weeks with supportive care; a normal INR and alertness mean no liver failure.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Uncomplicated acute hepatitis A without liver failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Supportive care at home with review of LFTs.

elim: For paracetamol toxicity.
No role in viral hepatitis.
For hepatitis B; hepatitis A is never chronic.
No liver failure present.

steps.x: **E. Supportive care at home with review of LFTs.** Acute hepatitis A = supportive; resolves in 2–3 weeks.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has acute hepatitis E confirmed by anti-HEV IgM. He has mild jaundice and is eating normally. He drinks 20 units of alcohol a week. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. His INR is 1.0. He is not immunosuppressed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Rest, hydration, avoid alcohol and monitor LFTs
questions.e: Acute hepatitis E is managed supportively with rest, fluids, alcohol avoidance and LFT monitoring; it is usually self-limiting.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Uncomplicated hepatitis E in an immunocompetent man.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Rest, hydration, avoid alcohol and monitor LFTs.

elim: No vaccine exists against hepatitis E.
Treats hepatitis B.
Not used for acute hepatitis E.
Treats hepatitis C.

steps.x: **D. Rest, hydration, avoid alcohol and monitor LFTs.** Hepatitis D and E: supportive care, avoid alcohol, monitor LFTs.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a positive HCV RNA PCR 8 weeks after a needlestick injury from a patient with hepatitis C. Anti-HCV was negative at the time of injury. He feels well. His ALT is 180 IU/L (10–50). His BP is 122/78 mmHg and pulse rate 70 bpm.
questions.q: According to his notes, which is the most appropriate management at this stage?
questions.e: Acute hepatitis C has no specific treatment beyond monitoring at this stage; some patients clear it, and those who do not get DAAs.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.

clues: negative at the time of injury
steps.x: New, acute hepatitis C infection, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Monitor HCV RNA and LFTs.

elim: No vaccine exists for hepatitis C.
He is well with no liver failure.
No role in viral hepatitis.
Treats hepatitis B, not C.

steps.x: **C. Monitor HCV RNA and LFTs.** Acute hepatitis C: monitor; chronic: DAAs.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man was treated for hepatitis C in 2004, before direct-acting antivirals were available. He had 48 weeks of weekly injections plus tablets, with fevers, low mood and anaemia. He now has a sustained virological response.
questions.q: Which regimen did he most likely receive?
questions.e: Before DAAs, hepatitis C was treated with PEGylated interferon (weekly injection) plus ribavirin (tablets), causing flu-like symptoms, depression and haemolytic anaemia.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Weekly injection and tablets with interferon side effects and ribavirin anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: PEGylated interferon plus ribavirin.

elim: Hepatitis B drugs.
Hepatitis B and HIV drug.
Autoimmune hepatitis treatment.
A DAA regimen, not available in 2004.

steps.x: **D. PEGylated interferon plus ribavirin.** Old hepatitis C regimen = PEG-interferon + ribavirin; now DAAs.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman is going to work for 6 months in a rural clinic in Bangladesh. She has had no travel vaccines. She is well. Her BP is 116/72 mmHg and pulse rate 68 bpm. She asks which vaccine will protect her against viral hepatitis from food and water.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate vaccine?
questions.e: Vaccines exist for hepatitis A and B only; hepatitis A is the food- and water-borne one.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Faeco-oral risk in a developing country.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitis A vaccine.

elim: Protects against tuberculosis.
No vaccine exists.
No vaccine exists; prevented by hepatitis B vaccine.
No vaccine exists in the UK.

steps.x: **B. Hepatitis A vaccine.** Vaccines exist for hepatitis A and B; none for C, D or E.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has just been diagnosed with hepatitis D superinfection on chronic hepatitis B. His female partner, who also injects drugs, has never been vaccinated. Her HBsAg and anti-HBc are negative. Her BP is 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to protect her from hepatitis D?
questions.e: Hepatitis D cannot exist without hepatitis B, so preventing HBV with vaccination also prevents HDV.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Uninfected, unvaccinated contact; HDV needs HBV to infect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitis B vaccination.

elim: No vaccine exists for hepatitis D.
Not used for prevention here.
Not a preventive treatment.
Treats hepatitis C.

steps.x: **A. Hepatitis B vaccination.** Prevent HBV and you prevent HDV.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man is newly diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B. He lives with his wife and two children aged 4 and 7. None of them has been tested or vaccinated. His ALT is 40 IU/L (10–50) and HBV DNA is low. His BP is 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step for his family?
o: Give all contacts hepatitis B immunoglobulin only
No action unless they develop jaundice
Test household and sexual contacts and vaccinate those not immune
questions.e: Contact screening is part of long-term hepatitis B care: test household and sexual contacts and vaccinate those who are not immune.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.

clues: None of them has been tested or vaccinated
steps.x: New chronic HBV case with untested household and sexual contacts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Test household and sexual contacts and vaccinate those not immune.

elim: HBIG is for acute exposures, not long-term protection.
Most infections are silent; screening is needed.
Treatment is only for infected people with active disease.
The children live with him and also need testing.

steps.x: **D. Test household and sexual contacts and vaccinate those not immune.** Hepatitis B: screen and vaccinate contacts; post-exposure prophylaxis after exposures.

questions.stem: A baby was born 3 days ago to a mother who is HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive. He received hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin 6 hours after birth. He is feeding well, with a heart rate of 136 bpm. His parents ask what happens next.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: A second dose of immunoglobulin now
Further vaccine doses at 1 to 2 months and 6 months
questions.e: After the birth dose of vaccine and HBIG within 12 to 24 hours, the baby completes the course with doses at 1 to 2 months and 6 months.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
High-risk baby who has had the birth dose; the course is not complete.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Further vaccine doses at 1 to 2 months and 6 months.

elim: One dose of HBIG at birth is enough.
One dose does not give lasting protection.
Not used for newborns.
Breastfeeding is safe after immunisation.

steps.x: **B. Further vaccine doses at 1 to 2 months and 6 months.** Baby of HBeAg+ mother: vaccine + HBIG at birth, then 1–2 months and 6 months.

questions.stem: A 19 year old student had hepatitis A 6 months ago. He was jaundiced for 2 weeks and then recovered fully. His ALT is now 22 IU/L (10–50). He asks why he will not become a long-term carrier, as his uncle has with hepatitis B.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: It is a non-enveloped RNA virus that causes acute, self-limiting infection
It mutates too quickly to be cleared
It only infects bile duct cells
questions.e: Hepatitis A (like E) is a non-enveloped RNA virus spread faeco-orally that causes acute, self-limiting inflammation without chronic carriage.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying process.
Acute illness that cleared completely, no chronic stage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It is a non-enveloped RNA virus that causes acute, self-limiting infection.

elim: That is hepatitis B, and it explains chronicity.
That is hepatitis C, and it causes chronicity.
That is hepatitis D.
It infects hepatocytes.

steps.x: **B. It is a non-enveloped RNA virus that causes acute, self-limiting infection.** Hepatitis A and E: non-enveloped RNA, faeco-oral, acute only.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had a kidney transplant 3 years ago and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. His ALT has been 150 to 200 IU/L (10–50) for 6 months. He eats a lot of cured pork. HEV RNA has been detectable in his blood on three occasions over 6 months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his persistent infection?
o: Hepatitis E integrating into hepatocyte DNA
questions.e: Hepatitis E is normally acute and self-limiting, but it can rarely become chronic in immunosuppressed patients such as transplant recipients.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying process.

clues: detectable in his blood on three occasions
steps.x: Persistent HEV RNA over 6 months in a transplant patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Immunosuppression allowing chronic hepatitis E.

elim: Hepatitis D needs hepatitis B.
HEV is an RNA virus that does not integrate.
Persistent viraemia reflects failed clearance.
No hepatitis E vaccine is used in the UK.

steps.x: **C. Immunosuppression allowing chronic hepatitis E.** Chronic hepatitis E occurs rarely, in the immunosuppressed.
